---
title: "Git and your course repository"
---

A handful of projects sit on your disk by now, from the hello page to the blog
page of the last chapter. Each exists in exactly one version. Overwrite
`src/index.ts` with something worse and yesterday's work is gone. This chapter
gives your projects a memory, and then a home on the internet.

## Give your to-do list a memory {#sec-git-init}

Open a terminal in your to-do list project and run:

```bash
git init
```

Git answers with one line:

```
Initialized empty Git repository in .../todo-list/.git/
```

If git also printed a long hint about `master`, run `git branch -m main` now.
The rest of this chapter assumes your branch is called `main`.

Now ask git what it sees:

```bash
git status
```

Every file that came with the starter is in the answer, plus whatever you
added yourself:

```
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	.agents/
	.claude
	.gitignore
	.vscode/
	assets/
	biome.json
	index.html
	package-lock.json
	package.json
	skills-lock.json
	src/
	tsconfig.json

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
```

Most terminals print that list in red. The heading **Untracked files** means
git can see them and is not looking after them yet.

One folder is missing. `node_modules` sits right there in the project, and git
does not mention it at all. Work out why before you read on.

## The file that keeps node_modules out {#sec-git-gitignore}

Open `.gitignore` in the project root. The starter ships it, and its first
lines are:

```
# Dependencies and generated output
node_modules/
dist/
coverage/
*.tsbuildinfo
```

Every line is a pattern for files and folders git pretends not to see.
`node_modules/` is on the list because it is not your work. `package.json`
already writes down which packages the project needs, and `npm install`
fetches them again on any computer in about a minute. The folder is also huge:
around 130 MB in a fresh starter, against a few kilobytes for everything you
wrote. `dist/` is out for the same reason, because `npm run build` recreates
it. Copy this `.gitignore` into every project and `node_modules` never lands
in a repository.

## Tell git who you are {#sec-git-identity}

Every saved version records who made it, so set that once per computer:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.address@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

The third line makes every future `git init` start on a branch called `main`,
which is what GitHub expects. Skip the first two and git refuses to commit
with "Please tell me who you are".

## Your first commit {#sec-git-commit}

Two commands turn the red list into a saved version:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add the to-do list with add, done, and delete"
```

The commit prints a summary of what it stored:

```
[main (root-commit) e5f982c] Add the to-do list with add, done, and delete
 14 files changed, 1705 insertions(+)
```

Run `git status` once more and the red list is gone:

```
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

Clean means the files on your disk and the last saved version are identical.

## Repositories and commits {#sec-git-repository}

A **repository** is a folder plus its history. `git init` created a hidden
`.git` folder next to your files, and that folder holds every version you ever
save. Delete `.git` and you have a plain folder again, history gone.

One saved version is a **commit**: a snapshot of every tracked file at one
moment, with your name, the time, and your message attached. All of it lives
on your disk so far. Nothing has been uploaded anywhere.

The word `add` is misleading. `git add` marks which changes belong in the next
commit, and `git commit` is what stores them. So you can fix three files,
commit two of them, and keep working on the third.

## Reading git status {#sec-git-status}

`git status` is the command you run most, so learn its three headings. Here is
a project showing two of them at once:

```
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   src/styles.css

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
	modified:   src/index.ts
```

* **Untracked files** are files git has never stored. New files start here.
* **Changes not staged for commit** are tracked files you edited since the
  last commit.
* **Changes to be committed** are the changes `git add` picked. The next
  `git commit` stores these and nothing else.

So `src/styles.css` goes into the next commit and the edit in `src/index.ts`
does not, until you `git add src/index.ts` too.

## The daily loop {#sec-git-loop}

Four commands, always in this order:

1. `git status` to see what changed.
2. `git add .` to pick the changes.
3. `git commit -m "..."` to save them with a message.
4. `git push` to send them to GitHub.

Commit often, whenever a small piece works. Ten small commits with clear
messages are worth far more than one commit called "homework" at midnight.

## Putting it on GitHub {#sec-git-github}

The commits live on your laptop, which is fine until the laptop dies. GitHub
keeps a copy and gives your teacher a link to read. If you have no account
yet, create one now at [github.com](https://github.com), then make an empty
repository:

1. Click the **+** in the top right, then **New repository**.
2. Name it, for example `creative-coding-2`.
3. Leave every box under "Initialize this repository" unticked, so the
   repository arrives with no README and no `.gitignore`.
4. Click **Create repository**.

GitHub now shows a page with a web address ending in `.git`. Connect your
local repository to it and send everything up:

```bash
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-name>/creative-coding-2.git
git push -u origin main
```

`origin` is the name your repository uses for "the copy on GitHub". The `-u`
tells git to remember the connection, so every later push is a bare
`git push`. The push ends with:

```
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
```

Reload the GitHub page and your files are there.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Git with buttons in VS Code

VS Code's **Source Control** view is git with a user interface. It lists your
changed files. The **+** next to a file runs `git add`, the message box with
the check mark runs `git commit`, and the sync arrows run `git push`. Use
whichever you like, and learn the commands anyway: they work in every terminal
on every computer, including the ones in the exam room.
:::

## One repository for the whole year {#sec-git-course-repo}

You get one repository for this course, not one per project, and it has a
fixed layout:

```
creative-coding-2/
├── .gitignore
├── coursework/
│   ├── 2026-09-15-hello-again/
│   └── 2026-09-22-click-counter/
├── homework/
│   └── 2026-09-22-simple-calculator/
└── projects/
    └── pixel-art-editor/
```

`coursework/` holds what you build together in class, `homework/` holds your
homework solutions, and `projects/` is for anything you make on your own.
Inside the first two, a folder name starts with the date of the lesson,
`YYYY-MM-DD`, followed by a short name in lowercase with hyphens. Dates
written that way sort themselves, so the newest work sits at the bottom.

Keep it tidy. Your teacher reads this repository, and a clean repository is
part of your grade: the layout above, folder names that say what a project is,
and commit messages someone else can understand.

::: {.research title="How do you write a commit message?"}
In the exercise below you write one commit message per project, and messages
like "stuff" and "asdf" will not do. Programmers have argued about this for
years and written the results down.

1. Find two named conventions for commit messages. What does each one ask you
   to write, and where did you find it?
2. `git log` prints the history. What does `git log --oneline` show instead,
   and what does it leave out?
3. You committed a file by mistake and afterwards added it to `.gitignore`,
   but git keeps reporting changes to it. Why does `.gitignore` not help here,
   and which command stops git tracking the file without deleting it from your
   disk?

For the exam, keep the convention you picked in your head. You will write
commit messages without a browser tab open.
:::

## Exercise: your course repository {#sec-git-exercise}

Build the repository you will use for the whole year, and move everything you
have written so far into it.

1. On GitHub, create the empty repository as described above, named
   `creative-coding-2`. Expected result: a page showing a web address that
   ends in `.git`.
2. Create a folder `creative-coding-2` next to your project folders, open a
   terminal in it, run `git init`, then
   `git remote add origin <the address from step 1>`.
3. Copy the `.gitignore` from one of your starter projects into the root of
   `creative-coding-2`. Expected result: `git status` lists `.gitignore` as
   untracked.
4. Create the folders `coursework`, `homework`, and `projects`. Git says
   nothing about empty folders, so `git status` does not change yet.
5. Move each project you have built so far into
   `coursework/YYYY-MM-DD-short-name/`, using the date of the lesson it
   belongs to. Anything you did as homework goes under `homework/` instead.
6. Delete the `node_modules` folder in every moved project. You are deleting
   downloads, not work: `npm install` brings it back whenever you want to run
   that project again. Expected result: your course folder shrinks by a few
   hundred megabytes.
7. Delete the hidden `.git` folder inside your to-do list project. A
   repository inside a repository confuses git.
8. Commit one project at a time, so the history reads like a list of your
   work: `git add coursework/2026-09-15-hello-again`, then `git commit -m "..."`
   with a message in the convention you picked in the research task. Expected
   result after the last one: `git status` prints "nothing to commit, working
   tree clean".
9. Send everything up with `git push -u origin main`.
10. Open the repository page and click into one of the project folders. Check
    that `src/index.ts` and `index.html` are there and `node_modules` is not.
    If `node_modules` did make it in, the `.gitignore` was missing when you
    committed, and your third research answer tells you how to undo that.
11. Your teacher hands out a form for the repository link. Fill it in.

From now on, every exercise starts inside `coursework/` or `homework/`, and
every lesson ends with a commit and a push.
